title: You Had Memories As A Baby (You Can't Reach Them)
sources: Yale News, 20 Mar 2025 (Yates et al., Science): fMRI of 26 infants 4 months to 2 years; hippocampal activity at first viewing predicted later recognition; strongest after age 1
Scientific American, "We Make Memories as Babies, So Why Do We Forget Them?": same study, memories encoded in infancy, retrieval as a possible explanation
Columbia news + WebMD (20 Mar 2025): same study, 26 infants
Akhtar et al. 2018 (BBC survey, 6,641 people): average earliest memory about 3.2 years; review PMC4104227: mean about 3.5 years
Guskjolen et al., Current Biology 2018 + SickKids press release: infant mice forgot a fear memory, light stimulation of tagged cells brought it back

lines.text: You had memories as a baby. You just can't reach them.
Ask anyone for their first memory, and it usually starts around age three.
Before that? Almost blank. Scientists call it infantile amnesia.
For decades, the explanation was simple: a baby brain was too young to record anything.
Then in twenty twenty-five, Yale scientists scanned twenty-six babies' brains while they looked at pictures.
The harder the memory center fired the first time, the more the baby recognized that picture later.
That worked best after about age one.
Baby mice point the same way: memories that seemed lost came back when scientists switched on the right brain cells.
So the memories may be saved. The hard part may be finding them.

vis.head: SAVED, NOT LOST?
vis.sub: FINDING THEM IS THE HARD PART

lines.text: Scientists still don't know how long baby memories last.
